title: A Positive Case for Faithfulness: Explanations Help Predict Model Behavior
claim: A faithful explanation should reveal the input factor that actually flipped the model's decision, unlike an explanation that omits it.
layout: 2 boxed panels left-to-right, arrow between, two explanation outcomes branching below
description: The figure shows two rounded boxes side by side, linked by a gray arrow pointing right. The left box holds a reference patient card (Sex M, Age 60, Cholesterol Elevated, Blood Pressure Normal), the question 'Does the patient have heart disease?', and a blue chat bubble answering 'No heart disease' beside a robot icon. Below that is a blue 'Explanation:' bubble. The right box shows a counterfactual patient with the same fields, but only Age: 30 is bold and the other fields are grayed out. Its answer is 'Heart disease'. From the explanation bubble, a green arrow goes down to a green box labeled 'Faithful explanation', which mentions age. A red curved arrow goes to a red box labeled 'Unfaithful explanation', which mentions only blood pressure. The eye goes first to the patient cards, then to the green and red outcomes.
caption: Faithful explanations should reveal decision-making criteria. An LLM assesses two patients for heart disease. The patients' profiles differ only in age. The LLM switches answers, indicating age is a determining factor. A faithful explanation should mention the influence of age.
abstract: LLM self-explanations are often presented as a promising tool for AI oversight, yet their faithfulness to the model's true reasoning process is poorly understood. Existing faithfulness metrics have critical limitations, typically relying on identifying unfaithfulness via adversarial prompting or detecting reasoning errors. These methods overlook the predictive value of explanations. We introduce Normalized Simulatability Gain (NSG), a general and scalable metric based on the idea that a faithful explanation should allow an observer to learn a model's decision-making criteria, and thus better predict its behavior on related inputs. We evaluate 18 frontier proprietary and open-weight models, e.g., Gemini 3, GPT-5.2, and Claude 4.5, on 7,000 counterfactuals from popular datasets covering health, business, and ethics. We find self-explanations substantially improve prediction of model behavior (11-37% NSG). Self-explanations also provide more predictive information than explanations generated by external models, even when those models are stronger. This implies an advantage from self-knowledge that external explanation methods cannot replicate. Our approach also reveals that, across models, 5-15% of self-explanations are highly misleading. Despite their imperfections, we show a positive case for self-explanations: they encode information that helps predict model behavior.
